source.title: MiniCPM: Unveiling the Potential of Small Language Models with Scalable Training Strategies
source.authors: Sheng-Ding Hu; Yuge Tu; Xu Han; Chaoqun He; Ganqu Cui; Xiang Long; Zhi Zheng; Yewei Fang; Yu-Xiang Huang; Weilin Zhao; Xinrong Zhang; Zhen Leng Thai; Kai Zhang; Chongyi Wang; Yuan Yao; Chenyang Zhao; Jie Zhou; Jie Cai; Zhongwu Zhai; Ning Ding; Chaochao Jia; Guo-Yang Zeng; Dahai Li; Zhi-Yuan Liu; Mao-Song Sun

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some appendix figure text is garbled, but the scaling-law sections are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out loss across model sizes and training-token amounts and fits scaling laws, using its WSD training setup.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports benchmark comparisons, but these do not test whether downstream performance is predictably related to pretraining loss or scale. Results cited from other papers are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains its own sweep of six model sizes (0.04B–2B), each decayed from stable-stage checkpoints at 10N–60N tokens, using WSD rather than per-run cosine schedules. It fits a Hoffmann-style L(N,D) on five held-out corpora and derives the compute-optimal allocation. That is a different method aimed at the same questions as V1, V3 and V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors say WSD lets them measure the data-model scaling law at linear rather than quadratic cost. They find a compute-optimal data-to-model ratio of about 192, much higher than Chinchilla's 20, while saying its trend with compute aligns with Hoffmann (slightly more emphasis on data). A rough Llama2 estimate (70–100) is closer to their value. They state they have not validated the law by training an LLM.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a WSD schedule and continued-training checkpoints to measure the model-data loss surface efficiently, and averages loss by bytes; it fits a Hoffmann-style model/data loss function and derives compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted exponents and derived allocation are reported across different evaluation corpora; fit exceptions occur at the last checkpoints of the 0.11B and 0.25B models.

fits_no_version.finding: Optimal batch size follows a power law in C4 loss: bs = 1.21e9 / L^6.24, fitted on 0.009B–0.17B models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal hyperparameters such as batch size scale as a power law of achieved loss.

fits_no_version.finding: Under Tensor Program (µP) scaling, the optimal learning rate stays about 0.01 from 0.04B to 0.5B and is checked at 2.1B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: With µP-style parameterisation the optimal learning rate transfers across model scale.

record.problems: The scaling sweep covers SLMs only, from 0.04B to 2B; the authors explicitly say they have not validated the scaling law by training an LLM. Some last-checkpoint fits are exceptions, and the comparison with Llama 2 is described as rough.
record.rows_left_out: No additional scaling-law rows omitted. Downstream benchmark tables were not extracted because they do not test predictability of downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss.

untested.parts: Several orders of magnitude: model sizes span about 1.8 orders and data 10N–60N per model; nothing above 2B.
No small-run fit is checked against much larger runs; the authors say LLM validation was not done.
Stability of the allocation exponent at LLM scale; the power form itself is assumed by the derivation rather than tested.
Not tested; shape is deliberately held similar across the sweep (Table 8).
Not tested; MoE, long-context and DPO variants have no scaling curves.
Not tested; benchmarks are only compared across models.

missing.what: Per-corpus fitted exponents, η (−0.33 to −0.00) and Dopt/Nopt at C=1e21 (95.60 to 833.95); one corpus has α=β=0.30, i.e. Chinchilla-like equal scaling.
Authors' rough estimate of the Llama2 compute-optimal data/model ratio, about 70–100 from Llama2 training curves, offered to explain the gap with Chinchilla's 20 as a configuration effect.

record.verdict_notes: The η power form is implied by the chosen L(N,D) form, so V3 support is about the direction and size of the split, not the form. The authors' 'aligns with Hoffmann' is loose: α>β implies data grows slightly faster than model size. Figure 10 text is garbled, so mapping η values to specific corpora is uncertain; only ranges are reported here. The scale range is narrow for a V1 'several orders of magnitude' claim.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests text language models with its own model and data sweep; it does not test all language-model setups or several orders of magnitude in scale.
No loss law fitted only on small runs is used to predict and then checked against substantially larger runs.
The reported compute-optimal relationship is based on six SLM sizes from 0.04B to 2B and the study's training and fitting setup; it does not validate the trend at LLM scale.
The study does not isolate depth, width, or other architecture changes at fixed parameter count to measure their effect on loss.
No other modality, repeated-data comparison, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling law is tested.
The benchmark results are not a study of predictable downstream-task improvement as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
The study does not systematically vary parameter-counting conventions, fitting procedures, or other setups to establish which choices cause the differences.

rows.subject: MiniCPM models (six sizes, 0.04B to 2B)
rows.size_stated: 0.04B to 2B; Appendix Figure 17 labels the sizes 0.031B, 0.11B, 0.25B, 0.49B, 0.85B, and 2.0B
rows.operation_detail: Fit held-out loss as a function of model size and training data size using WSD-trained checkpoints; losses were averaged by bytes.

conditions.value: Chinese Wikihow, English Wikihow, Code, Chinese Yayi Corpus, Ultratext
10N to 60N stable-training checkpoints, followed by decay

rows.measure: Held-out loss fitted against model size N and data size D
rows.value: Fitted form: L(N,D) = C_N N^-α + C_D D^-β + L0. Across datasets, average α = 0.29 and β = 0.23; the authors state β < α for all evaluation corpora.
rows.note: Aggregate result reported across five evaluation corpora and six model sizes; the paper says the fits are satisfactory overall, with exceptions recorded in R3.
rows.check: Value is right. For V1, losses are fitted by L(N,D) with power terms on every corpus; the authors call the fit satisfying apart from R3's exceptions. For V7, the per-corpus exponents in Fig. 10 differ (α about 0.19–0.37, β about 0.17–0.34). The scale span is under two orders of magnitude in N and only 6x in D per model, which this row should state.

rows.subject: MiniCPM models (six sizes, 0.04B to 2B)
rows.operation_detail: Derive compute-optimal model and data sizes from the fitted loss law under C = 6ND.
rows.measure: Compute-optimal model-to-data allocation as a function of compute
rows.baseline: Hoffmann et al. (2022): data-to-model ratio of 20
rows.value: Average α = 0.29, β = 0.23, K2 = 0.01, and η = -0.10; the authors say the data-to-model ratio is 192 on average and that its trend with compute aligns with Hoffmann et al. (2022).
rows.note: The derived allocation gives slightly greater emphasis to data scaling than model scaling. The authors note a large difference in the ratio from Hoffmann et al., while estimating that a rough comparison using Llama 2 may bring the ratios closer.
rows.check: The power-of-compute form for Nopt/Dopt follows from the fitted functional form, so it is not tested independently. With α>β on every corpus, η is negative (average −0.10), so data grows slightly faster than model size. That is near Hoffmann's equal split, opposite to Kaplan's, and not exactly equal. The ratio of about 192 vs Hoffmann's 20 is the V7-relevant fact. The per-corpus spread (η from −0.33 to −0.00; Dopt/Nopt at C=1e21 from 95.6 to 833.95) is not recorded.

source_check.correct: State: observed for the derived power-of-compute allocation and setup dependence. Average α=0.29, β=0.23, K²=0.01, η=−0.10; data grows slightly faster than parameters. The optimum is derived from the fitted loss surface, without an independent allocation sweep.
source_check.locator_found: Section 4.5, Equations 2–3 and accompanying discussion; Figure 10.
source_check.problem: The reported allocation and setup differences appear clearly; differing from prior allocation coefficients does not make these effects partial.

rows.subject: MiniCPM 0.11B and 0.25B models, last checkpoints
rows.operation_detail: Compare fitted data-scaling curves with measured losses at the last checkpoints.
rows.measure: Fit quality of held-out loss curves
rows.value: The authors state that the fit is satisfying except for the last checkpoints of the 0.11B and 0.25B models.
rows.note: The paper reports these exceptions together and does not specify which evaluation corpora account for them.
rows.check: This also bears on V1, as a fit-quality exception. The size of the deviation and the corpora involved are not given, so the effect is small or uncertain.

rows.subject: 0.036B model
rows.operation_detail: Fit an optimal-loss envelope for continued training at fixed model size, where loss for token amount D is achieved by WSD(D, 0.1D).
rows.measure: Loss versus training compute for the fixed-size model
rows.value: The authors find the power-law fit, L(C) = βC^-α + L0, fits better; the 0.036B model can match the 0.17B model with about 4 times the training compute.
rows.note: This is a fixed-model-size continued-training result, not a small-run extrapolation test.
rows.check: OK. This is a single fixed-size 0.036B model whose loss envelope over training compute is fitted better by a power law plus constant than by an exponential. The '4x compute to match 0.17B' figure is a comparison, not a scaling result.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.3, Effective Data Scaling with WSD LRS; Figure 6; Appendix B.2 and Figure 16.

relationships.condition: MiniCPM SLMs 0.03B–2B, WSD-decayed checkpoints, five held-out corpora; fixed 0.036B continued training
relationships.reason: The power-law L(N,D) fits all five corpora (R1), and a power law beats an exponential for the fixed-size loss envelope (R4).
relationships.display_finding: The joint parameter-and-token power law fit all five corpora, and a power law outperformed an exponential for the fixed-size continued-training loss envelope.
